JSON: Name: mwnet_wavelet_memorybank Title: Memory-bank and adaptive-wavelet convolution network for spatiotemporal segmentation of long ultrasound videos Short Hypothesis: Integrating adaptive wavelet-based multiscale convolution, a long–short-term memory bank, and high-frequency-aware feature fusion into an encoder–decoder network will improve boundary localization and small-object segmentation in long ultrasound videos, producing higher Dice and IoU and lower MAE than equivalent backbones without one or more of these components. Related Work: Prior work on ultrasound/video segmentation includes: encoder–decoder CNNs (U-Net variants) that yield strong local detail but limited long-range temporal modeling; transformer-based backbones that capture global context but under-utilize high-frequency boundary detail and can introduce redundancy; plug-in wavelet or frequency modules that augment encoders or skip connections but are treated as isolated components rather than jointly optimized across encoder and decoder; temporal models based on ConvLSTM or short-term frame aggregation that capture adjacent-frame dynamics but fail to model long-range dependencies or suffer memory growth; and memory-bank approaches that preserve longer history but can become redundant, noisy, or compute-intensive. Feature fusion research has focused on learned upsampling operators and content-aware reassembly but often does not explicitly separate or adaptively weight low-/high-frequency components for boundary-sensitive fusion. Collectively, limitations are (1) insufficient, coherent use of multi-resolution high-frequency information across encoder and decoder, (2) poor scalability or redundancy management in long-term memory banks, and (3) lack of HF-aware adaptive fusion that targets boundary and small-object recovery. Abstract: We address segmentation failures in long ultrasound videos caused by blurred boundaries, speckle noise, and small-object loss. We propose an end-to-end network that combines adaptive wavelet-based multiscale convolution in the encoder, a long–short-term memory bank for controlled temporal aggregation, and a high-frequency-aware decoder fusion that applies adaptive low/high-pass filtering during upsampling. The encoder uses cascaded adaptive wavelet decompositions to produce multiresolution low- and high-frequency feature maps while expanding receptive field without large kernels. A constrained long–short-term memory bank integrates nearby-frame ConvLSTM outputs with a compressed long-term store via cross-attention and similarity-driven updates. The decoder’s adaptive wavelet filters reweight and fuse multiscale features to emphasize boundary-sensitive high-frequency components. The main contribution is a unified pipeline that jointly (1) extracts HF-sensitive spatiotemporal features, (2) preserves long-range history with bounded memory, and (3) fuses multiscale features with explicit HF adaptation. The expected outcome is improved boundary accuracy and small-object segmentation on long ultrasound video benchmarks compared with conventional CNN, transformer and memory-bank baselines. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Thyroid Nodule dataset: 64 videos, 5,611 frames, split train/val/test = 40/10/14 videos; (2) VTUS: 100 videos, 9,342 frames, split 70/0/30 videos; (3) TG3K: 16 videos, 3,585 frames, split train/val/test = 12/2/2 videos; (4) CAMUS echocardiography: 1,000 sequences, split 700/100/200. Baselines: UNet, Swin-UNet, SegFormer, ConvNeXt backbone with identical decoder, MemSAM, Vivim (video Mamba-based), FreqFusion frequency-aware fusion. Proposed variants: (A) full MWNet; (B) MWNet without WTConv (replace with ConvNeXt stages); (C) MWNet without memory bank (remove long-term store and ConvLSTM temporal fusion); (D) MWNet with HFF replaced by bilinear upsampling; (E) MWNet with fixed wavelet bases (Haar, Daubechies, Symlet) instead of adaptive wavelet. Metrics: Dice coefficient, IoU, MAE, precision, recall, boundary F1, inference time (ms/frame), GPU memory (peak). Training/evaluation setup: input resized to 512×512, AdamW optimizer lr=1e-4 with linear warmup and poly decay, batch size 2, up to 180k iterations, ImageNet-pretrained backbone. Evaluate each model with three independent seeds and report mean±std. Statistical tests: paired t-test comparing MWNet vs best baseline per dataset (alpha=0.05). Ablations: measure metric delta for each variant (B–E) relative to (A). Additional experiments: (i) memory length sweep (short/long-term lengths = {2,4,8,16}) and section length sweep {10,20,30,40,50}; (ii) cross-dataset generalization: train on Thyroid Nodule and test on VTUS/TG3K; (iii) runtime/memory profiling on NVIDIA RTX 4090 at batch size 1. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: adaptive wavelet parameter learning may be unstable and converge to identity filters or overfit to noise; the memory bank may accumulate stale or inconsistent features leading to drift; ConvLSTM temporal fusion can fail when frame-to-frame variability is extreme. Data and evaluation biases: annotations may be inconsistent across frames and datasets; datasets biased toward particular probe types, anatomies, or imaging settings may reduce generalization. Scalability and compute: adaptive wavelet decompositions and attention-based memory updates increase computational and memory cost, limiting applicability in real-time or low-resource environments. Limits to generalization: the method may underperform on modalities with fundamentally different noise/statistics or on videos with extremely low temporal redundancy; small-object improvements may not transfer when objects are below sensor resolution. Evaluation constraints: improvements measured on curated benchmarks may not reflect performance in intraoperative or multi-center clinical deployments.
